title: Unit 2 test: Force and Translational Dynamics
author: cm-2
directions: This practice unit test has two sections: 12 multiple-choice questions (25 minutes) and 2 free-response questions (35 minutes). Any calculator is allowed. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units, and state your positive direction where it matters. Record raw points with the key; they are a practice tally, not an AP® score.

parts.directions: Choose the best answer for each question. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and neglect air resistance unless a question describes a drag force.

items.prompt: A 1.0 m rod lies along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 1.0 m. Its linear density is λ(x) = 2.0 + 3.0x, with λ in kg/m and x in meters. Where is its center of mass?
items.rationale: M = ∫ from 0 to 1.0 of (2.0 + 3.0x) dx = 2.0 + 1.5 = 3.5 kg and ∫ from 0 to 1.0 of x(2.0 + 3.0x) dx = 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.0 kg·m, so x_cm = 2.0/3.5 = 0.57 m, right of the middle because the right end is denser.

distractorNotes.A: This is the midpoint, which would be correct only for a uniform rod.
distractorNotes.C: This keeps only the 3.0x term, as if λ = 3.0x, which gives two-thirds of the length.
distractorNotes.D: This mirrors the correct answer to the wrong side of the midpoint.

items.prompt: A block is given a quick shove up a rough incline. After it leaves the hand, it slides up the incline and slows down. Which forces act on the block while it slides up?
choices: Gravity, the normal force and a force up the incline that keeps it moving
Gravity, the normal force and kinetic friction up the incline
Gravity and the normal force only
Gravity, the normal force and kinetic friction down the incline
items.rationale: Once the hand lets go, only the Earth (gravity) and the incline (normal force and friction) touch or pull on the block. Kinetic friction opposes the block's motion relative to the surface, so it points down the incline.

distractorNotes.A: No force keeps an object moving; the shove ended when contact ended, and the block coasts on its velocity.
distractorNotes.B: Friction opposes the sliding, which is up the incline, so friction points down the incline.
distractorNotes.C: The incline is rough, so kinetic friction acts while the block slides.

items.prompt: A 0.40 kg ball falls freely toward the ground. What force does the ball exert on the Earth?
choices: Zero, because the ball is in free fall
About 10^−24 N, because the Earth's mass is so large
items.rationale: The Earth pulls the ball down with mg = (0.40 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 3.9 N. By Newton's third law, the ball pulls the Earth with a force of the same size in the opposite direction: 3.9 N upward.

distractorNotes.B: The partner force points opposite the Earth's pull on the ball, so it is upward, toward the ball.
distractorNotes.C: Free fall means gravity is the only force on the ball; the interaction, and so its third-law partner, still exists.
distractorNotes.D: The Earth's large mass makes its acceleration tiny (about 10^−24 m/s^2), not the force on it.

items.prompt: A hockey puck slides at constant velocity across a horizontal surface. Three horizontal forces act on it. Two of them are F_1 = (3.0 i + 2.0 j) N and F_2 = (−5.0 i + 1.0 j) N. What is the third force?
choices: There is no definite third force, because a moving puck needs no balance of forces.
items.rationale: Constant velocity means zero net force (Newton's first law), so F_3 = −(F_1 + F_2) = −(−2.0 i + 3.0 j) N = (2.0 i − 3.0 j) N.

distractorNotes.A: This is F_1 + F_2, the sum that F_3 must cancel, not F_3 itself.
distractorNotes.D: The first law applies to constant velocity as well as to rest: the net force must be zero.

items.prompt: The graph shows the net horizontal force on a 1.5 kg cart that starts from rest at t = 0 on a level track. What is the cart's greatest speed between t = 0 and t = 5.0 s?
items.rationale: The velocity increases while the force is positive, so the greatest speed is at t = 4.0 s, where the force reaches zero. The area under the graph from 0 to 4.0 s is (6.0 N)(2.0 s) + ½(2.0 s)(6.0 N) = 18 N·s, so v_max = 18 N·s/1.5 kg = 12 m/s.

distractorNotes.A: This uses only the area from 0 to 2.0 s, but the force is still positive until 4.0 s.
distractorNotes.C: This is the speed at t = 5.0 s, after the negative force has slowed the cart.
distractorNotes.D: This counts the area below the axis as positive, adding it instead of subtracting it.

items.prompt: Block P (2.0 kg) and block Q (4.0 kg) sit on a frictionless table, joined by a light string. A horizontal force of 30 N pulls block P, and Q trails behind. What is the tension in the string?
items.rationale: Both blocks: a = 30 N/6.0 kg = 5.0 m/s^2. The string alone accelerates Q: T = (4.0 kg)(5.0 m/s^2) = 20 N.

distractorNotes.A: This is the net force on P, (2.0 kg)(5.0 m/s^2); the tension pulls Q, not P, forward.
distractorNotes.B: This splits the pull equally, ignoring the different masses.
distractorNotes.C: The string pulls back on P, so it carries less than the full 30 N.

items.prompt: A satellite orbits at an altitude equal to Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its location?
items.rationale: The distance from Earth's center is 2R, and g ∝ 1/r^2, so g = (9.80 m/s^2)/2^2 = 2.45 m/s^2.

distractorNotes.C: Gravity weakens with distance from Earth's center; an orbiting satellite is not beyond its reach.
distractorNotes.D: This divides by 3^2, measuring 3R from the center.

items.prompt: A 10 kg box rests on a level floor with μ_s = 0.40 and μ_k = 0.30. A worker pushes horizontally on it with a force of 35 N. What is the friction force on the box?
items.rationale: The maximum static friction is μ_s mg = 0.40(98 N) = 39 N. The 35 N push is less, so the box stays at rest and static friction matches the push: 35 N.

distractorNotes.A: μ_k mg applies only once the box slides, and this box does not slide.
distractorNotes.B: μ_s mg is the largest possible static friction, not the friction that is needed here.
distractorNotes.D: Friction must balance the push for the box to stay at rest.

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg mass hangs from a spring (k = 98 N/m) attached to the ceiling of an elevator. The elevator accelerates upward at 2.2 m/s^2, and the mass moves with it. By how much is the spring stretched?
items.rationale: With up positive, kΔx − mg = ma, so Δx = m(g + a)/k = (0.50)(12.0)/98 = 0.061 m = 6.1 cm.

distractorNotes.A: This is the stretch when the elevator is not accelerating, mg/k.
distractorNotes.C: This uses g − a, as if the elevator accelerated downward.
distractorNotes.D: This uses only ma/k and leaves out the weight.

items.prompt: A 0.25 kg ball is released from rest in a fluid that exerts a drag force bv with b = 0.50 kg/s. Ignore buoyancy. What is its speed 0.50 s after release?

distractorNotes.B: This is the terminal speed, which the ball only approaches.
distractorNotes.C: This assumes the ball reaches half its terminal speed after one time constant.
distractorNotes.D: This uses e^(−2), as if two time constants had passed.

items.prompt: A 60 kg rider passes through the bottom of a vertical loop of radius 15 m at 18 m/s. What force does the seat exert on the rider there?
items.rationale: At the bottom the center is above the rider: F_N − mg = mv^2/r, so F_N = 60(9.8 + 18^2/15) = 60(31.4) = 1.9 × 10^3 N, upward.

distractorNotes.A: This is the rider's weight, which ignores the centripetal acceleration.
distractorNotes.B: This is mv^2/r alone, leaving out the weight.
distractorNotes.C: This subtracts the weight, as if the rider were at the top of the loop.

items.prompt: A stone on a string moves in a horizontal circle on a frictionless table. Its speed is doubled and the radius of its circle is halved. By what factor does the tension in the string change?
items.rationale: The tension supplies the centripetal force, T = mv^2/r. Doubling v multiplies v^2 by 4, and halving r multiplies 1/r by 2, so T becomes 8 times as large.

distractorNotes.A: This treats the force as proportional to v and ignores the change in radius.
distractorNotes.B: This accounts for the doubled speed but not the smaller radius.
distractorNotes.D: This doubles the effect of the radius as well, as if T depended on 1/r^2.

parts.directions: Show your reasoning and include units. Question 1 is worth 12 points and Question 2 is worth 8 points.

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg block rests on a level floor. The coefficients of friction between the block and the floor are μ_s = 0.40 and μ_k = 0.25. Starting at t = 0, a horizontal force that grows steadily with time, F(t) = 4.0t (F in newtons, t in seconds), pulls on the block. Take the direction of the pull as positive.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw and label a free-body diagram of the block at an instant after it has started to slide. Draw the arrows to show the relative sizes of the vertical forces.

rubric.criterion: Draws four forces: gravity down, the normal force up, the pull F in the + direction and kinetic friction opposite F; no extra forces.
Shows the normal force and gravity with equal lengths and labels every force.

parts.answer: Gravity (down) and the normal force (up), equal in length; the pull F forward and kinetic friction f_k backward.
steps: Only the Earth (gravity), the floor (normal force and friction) and the rope (pull) interact with the block.
Nothing vertical accelerates, so F_N = mg = 19.6 N.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the time at which the block starts to slide.

rubric.criterion: Sets the pull equal to the maximum static friction: 4.0t = μ_s mg = 7.84 N.
Finds t = 1.96 s (accept 1.9–2.0 s).

steps: Until then static friction matches the pull; slipping starts when the pull reaches μ_s mg = 0.40(2.0)(9.8) = 7.84 N.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the block's acceleration a against time from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s. Label the values of a just after sliding begins and at t = 4.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Shows a = 0 from t = 0 until sliding begins at about 2.0 s.
Shows a jump at that time to about 1.5 m/s^2 (accept 1.4–1.5 m/s^2).
Shows a straight, rising line from there to about 5.6 m/s^2 at t = 4.0 s (accept 5.5–5.6 m/s^2).

parts.answer: Zero until t = 1.96 s, then a jump to 1.47 m/s^2, then a straight line rising with slope 2.0 m/s^3 to 5.55 m/s^2 at t = 4.0 s.
steps: While sliding, a = (F − μ_k mg)/m = (4.0t − 4.9)/2.0 = 2.0t − 2.45 m/s^2.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Starting from Newton's second law, derive an expression for the block's acceleration while it slides, and use it to calculate the block's speed at t = 4.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Writes 4.0t − μ_k mg = ma, giving a(t) = 2.0t − 2.45 (m/s^2).
Integrates a(t) from the start of sliding (1.96 s) to 4.0 s with v = 0 at 1.96 s.
Gets v = 7.2 m/s (accept 7.1–7.2 m/s).

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain how the speed in part (d) can be found from your graph in part (c). Then explain, in terms of forces, why the acceleration changes suddenly when the block starts to slide even though the pull changes smoothly.

rubric.criterion: States that the speed equals the area under the a–t graph from the start of sliding to 4.0 s, a trapezoid ½(1.47 + 5.55)(2.04) ≈ 7.2 m/s, which agrees with part (d).
Explains that friction drops from μ_s mg = 7.84 N to μ_k mg = 4.9 N when sliding begins, so the net force jumps from 0 to about 2.9 N.

parts.answer: The change in velocity is the area under the acceleration–time graph: ½(1.47 + 5.55)(4.0 − 1.96) = 7.2 m/s, matching part (d). The pull is continuous, but friction falls suddenly from 7.84 N (maximum static) to 4.9 N (kinetic) when the block breaks free, so the net force, and with it the acceleration, jumps from zero to 2.94 N/2.0 kg = 1.47 m/s^2.
steps: Δv = ∫ a dt is the area under the a–t graph.
Net force just after slipping: 7.84 N − 4.9 N = 2.94 N.

items.prompt: Two identical coins rest on a flat, horizontal turntable, as shown. Coin A is 0.10 m from the axis and coin B is 0.20 m from the axis. The coefficient of static friction between each coin and the turntable is μ_s = 0.50. Starting from rest, the turntable's rotation is sped up so slowly that at every moment each coin moves in uniform circular motion with the turntable's period T.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Without using equations, determine which coin starts to slide first as the rotation speeds up. Explain your reasoning.

rubric.criterion: Chooses coin B, the coin farther from the axis.
Explains that at the same period B moves faster around a larger circle and needs a larger inward force, while the largest friction available is the same for both identical coins.

parts.answer: Coin B. Both coins go around in the same time, but B travels a circle twice as large, so it moves faster and needs more inward force. Static friction supplies that force, and its maximum is the same for the two identical coins, so B reaches the limit first.
steps: The inward force needed grows with the speed and size of the circle.
Identical coins on the same surface have the same maximum static friction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the shortest period T_min at which a coin at distance r from the axis does not slide. Express your answer in terms of r, μ_s and g.

rubric.criterion: Identifies static friction as the only horizontal force and writes f_s = mv^2/r with v = 2πr/T, so f_s = 4π^2mr/T^2.
Applies the limit f_s ≤ μ_s mg (with F_N = mg).
Solves to T_min = 2π√(r/(μ_s g)).

steps: So T^2 ≥ 4π^2r/(μ_s g), and T_min = 2π√(r/(μ_s g)); the mass cancels.

parts.label: c

rubric.criterion: Finds T_min = 0.90 s for coin A and 1.3 s (1.27 s) for coin B.

parts.answer: Coin A: 0.90 s; coin B: 1.27 s.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how your results in parts (b) and (c) support or contradict your answer to part (a).

rubric.criterion: Explains that T_min grows with r, so coin B's limit (1.27 s) is reached first as the period falls from large values, which agrees with part (a).
Notes that the mass cancels in part (b), consistent with the reasoning that the needed force and the available friction both scale with the coin's mass.

parts.answer: They support it. Speeding up shortens the period, and T_min = 2π√(r/(μ_s g)) is larger for larger r, so the period falls to coin B's limit of 1.27 s before it reaches coin A's 0.90 s: B slides first. The mass cancels, matching the reasoning that both the needed inward force and the available friction are proportional to the coin's mass.
steps: The period decreases as the turntable speeds up, so the larger T_min is reached first.
